patterns.title: Aid money that goes back to companies in the donor country
patterns.summary:
Tied aid is aid that must be spent on goods or services from the country that gave it. Eurodad, a European network of groups working on debt and aid, counted about $26.9 billion of tied aid in 2018, or 21% of bilateral and EU aid. Its total for formal and informal tying together is at least $32.3 billion and possibly up to $37.9 billion. It puts the direct short-term cost of tying at $2 billion to $7 billion.

Aid can be reported as untied and the contracts can still go home. Eurodad reports that 52% of untied contract awards reported in 2018 went to suppliers in the donor's own country, and over 80% for nine donors. Only 11% went to suppliers in the least developed countries. Eurodad names large tender sizes, little notice in local media and little communication in local languages as barriers for local firms.

The OECD, whose aid committee tracks these numbers, reports that 82.3% of bilateral aid was reported as untied in 2020, a record, mainly because of higher shares for Japan and the United States. That leaves 17.7% not reported as untied (100 minus 82.3). It also reports that donor-country suppliers won 52% of contract value in 2019-20, down from 57% in 2017-18, and 37% of contracts by number, down from 40%. By donor, the share of contracts by number ranged from 0% to 94%. Australia and Hungary gave over 99% of contract value to their own suppliers. For aid covered by the OECD's untying recommendation, Greece reported 5% untied, the Slovak Republic 13%, Poland 17%, Austria 19% and Hungary 40%.
patterns.implications: The OECD gives reasons other than favouritism. Australia carries out 70% of its contracts in neighbouring small island states, whose economies are small and markets remote. Some donors buy through partner organisations based at home, which may be local subsidiaries of international companies. Donors also work in fields where they are active: 37% of French contracts were in water and 64% of US contracts in health. Local markets in fragile places can have too little supply and competition. The OECD also discusses barriers that developing-country firms face. Eurodad says the threat of tying is undiminished since 2018 and may be getting worse, and asks that the recommendation be widened to cover informal tying. These reports do not show how much of this spending harmed or helped any one place.

patterns.title: Aid that rises and falls with votes at the UN
patterns.summary:
Two studies measure aid against UN politics. Kuziemko and Werker (Journal of Political Economy, 2006) studied developing countries, using US aid data for 1946-2001 and UN aid data for 1960-2001. They find that when a country rotates onto the UN Security Council, its US aid rises 59% and its UN aid 8%. Aid rises sharply in the year of election and returns to its earlier level almost immediately after the term ends; UN aid takes until the second year after. For a typical developing member they estimate an extra $16 million from the US and $1 million from the UN. In years when the council was most in the news, measured by New York Times coverage, those become $45 million and $8 million.

Dreher and colleagues (International Studies Quarterly, 2018) studied 2,043 Chinese projects in 50 African countries committed in 2000-2012. Their abstract says China's aid-like money is driven mainly by foreign policy and its less generous loans by economic interests. Chinese grants rise the more closely a country votes with China at the UN General Assembly. For China's aid-like money as a whole, that voting link is not statistically significant. China gives less official money to countries that recognise Taiwan. The authors find that China and Western donors use these types of money for similar aims.

A column by Michael Moran on NBC News gives single cases. It says Yemen voted against sanctioning war over Kuwait in 1990, that the US told it within days not to expect $70 million in pledged aid, and that Saudi Arabia cancelled another $100 million and expelled 800,000 Yemeni workers. Kuziemko and Werker also report the US aid cut but date the vote to 1991. The column says US aid to Jordan, whose king felt he could not side against Saddam Hussein, fell from $993 million in 1990 to just over $200 million two years later, and that food riots and a deep recession followed. It describes Jordan's stance, not a UN vote. On 20 December 2017, before a General Assembly vote on Jerusalem, President Trump said of aid recipients: "They take hundreds of millions of dollars and even billions of dollars, and then they vote against us." He added: "Well, we're watching those votes. Let them vote against us. We'll save a lot. We don't care." US ambassador Nikki Haley said the US "will be taking names" (Al Jazeera).
patterns.implications: These studies show that aid moves with UN seats and votes. They measure money and timing, and do not show what any government promised in private. Kuziemko and Werker write that their results support the bribery explanation over two other explanations they tested, and that they could not directly test whether the aid changed votes. Dreher and colleagues also find China's aid-like money goes more to poorer countries, so politics is not the only driver. No reply from the US or Chinese governments to these studies was found.

patterns.title: Donors decide what most of the WHO's money pays for
patterns.summary:
The World Health Organization gets dues from member states and voluntary money from governments and private givers. The WHO says voluntary money has been more than three-quarters of its financing in recent years, and that 87% of voluntary money in 2022-2023 was tightly earmarked, meaning tied to set programme areas and time limits. A 2025 BMJ Group press release gives higher shares, around nine-tenths of income voluntary and almost all of that earmarked. CIDRAP, a health news service, gives about 90% and roughly 90%.

The press release describes a BMJ Global Health paper by researchers at Queen Mary University of London on 640 Gates Foundation grants to the WHO, worth $5.5 billion, from 2000 to 2024. More than 80% ($4.5 billion) went to infectious diseases, and almost 60% ($3.2 billion) to polio. Health systems strengthening got $37.4 million (0.7%) and water and sanitation $11.8 million (0.2%). Less than 1% went to non-communicable diseases. The press release says the foundation supplied 9.5% of WHO revenue in 2010-2023, making it the second-largest source in recent years. Devex reported US funding of $893 million (20% of the budget) and Gates funding of $531 million (12%) for 2018-2019, and that Gates was 45% of the WHO's non-governmental money.
patterns.implications: The authors say areas donors favour receive more than they need. They also say it is easy to blame major donors, and point to member states' failure to raise their dues over four decades as the reason the WHO depends on them. Member states have approved raising dues to cover 50% of the WHO's base budget by 2030 (WHO). The WHO rejected the idea that donors set its agenda: "No, our agenda is very clear, and it has been for decades, before they existed as a foundation," its senior external relations officer Cintia Diaz-Herrera told Devex in 2020. Devex reports that the WHO will not accept money for activities outside the plans set by member states. The WHO told CIDRAP it "greatly appreciates its long-standing collaboration with the Gates Foundation," and that the partnership has also focused on strengthening health systems. A foundation spokesperson told CIDRAP: "Philanthropy can make an important but limited contribution, and we're glad to do our part," and that its funding "represents a small share of WHO's overall funding." Lawrence Gostin of Georgetown University told Devex: "The big concerns are that the Gates Foundation isn't fully transparent and accountable."

patterns.title: Funds that buy old debt and sue in New York and London
patterns.summary:
When a country cannot pay, most lenders usually accept a reduced deal. A holdout refuses and sues for the full amount. A vulture fund is the critics' name for a fund that buys defaulted debt to do this. An ECB working paper (no. 2135, 2018) by Schumacher, Trebesch and Enderlein counted 158 cases against 34 defaulting governments from 1976 to 2010: 130 in US courts (82.3%), 23 in the UK (14.6%) and 5 in arbitration. New York law governs almost half of outstanding sovereign bonds (White & Case, 2024) or over 50% (Insurance Journal, 2026).

The share of restructurings that drew lawsuits rose from about 5% in the 1980s to 30-50% after 2000. Of 148 cases where the creditor is known, 79 were filed by funds, 38 by banks and the rest by other commercial creditors. Since 2000, 65% of cases were started by distressed debt funds. Funds tried to seize assets in 56% of their cases, other creditors in 28%.

In Elliott v. Peru, Elliott blocked an interest payment passing through Euroclear in September 2000, and Peru settled at face value, sending about $58 million. In the Republic of Congo, the paper says, creditors holding under $500 million blocked the country's entire oil exports for years. Argentina faced 182 lawsuits in one New York court, placed no international bond from January 2002 to April 2016, and paid holdouts more than $10 billion in 2016; Elliott's unit NML Capital alone held over $600 million in principal claims.
patterns.implications:
The same paper finds most seizure attempts failed in court, but that they raised the nuisance value of the suit. Returns sometimes reach 300% or more, and in some cases were zero or negative. Governments facing seizure attempts were about 23 percentage points less likely to place bonds or loans abroad, and those facing lawsuits about 16 points; with controls the drop is about 14-24%. From 2000 to 2010 no government being sued in London or New York placed a bond there in the same year.

New York has had two kinds of bill. The Sovereign Debt Stability Act, unveiled in March 2024, would set up a restructuring process and cap what creditors recover in some relief schemes at what the US government would get (White & Case). Investor groups including the Institute of International Finance replied that developing countries "could be pushed toward debt distress" and called it "a major blow to New York law's position as the gold standard." Critics cited by White & Case say borrowers could move contracts to other places and that the bill raises US constitutional issues. A 2025-26 restructuring bill, A7786, was last sent to committee in January 2026, and BillTrack50 lists it as dead.

The narrower bill, S1477, would let courts dismiss claims on foreign government debt bought mainly to sue, and lower the 9% interest on some judgments. Assemblymember Jessica González-Rojas said: "We are going after the bad actors." SIFMA, MFA, the Creditor Rights Coalition and the Business Council of New York State opposed it; MFA said it "would increase the cost of capital for sovereign borrowers." It passed the state Senate in June 2025 and died in the Assembly. It passed the Senate again on 2 June 2026 and was sent to the Assembly's judiciary committee. The state's legislature website lists it there, not passed.

patterns.title: Who holds the debt, and the rich-country law it runs under
patterns.summary:
Debt Justice, a UK campaign group, counted $900 billion in external debt payments by 88 lower-income countries for 2020 to 2025, using World Bank data. Private lenders other than Chinese ones got 39% ($354 billion), multilateral lenders 34% ($304 billion), other governments 14% ($125 billion) and Chinese public and private lenders 13% ($117 billion). The amounts for 2020-2023 are payments made. The amounts for 2024 and 2025 are scheduled payments on debts contracted by the end of 2023, not payments made, and leave out loans taken since then.

The owners of the bonds are hard to name. Debt Justice writes that "there is no publicly accessible information on who owns bonds." In December 2025 it and Christian Aid listed known holders of bonds of 15 lower-income countries, using Refinitiv data that covers only 23% of ownership. BlackRock has $3,321 million, J.P. Morgan $1,168 million, Goldman Sachs $1,089 million, UBS $798 million and PIMCO $795 million. They estimate BlackRock and its clients could make $2,137 million more than if they had lent to the US government, an average of 64% more on this measure, assuming the bonds were held from issue. Zambia and Sri Lanka are not among the 15.

Crises have also shown some holders. In Zambia, Debt Justice's earlier name, Jubilee Debt Campaign, reported in 2022 that BlackRock was the largest known holder with $220 million, 7% of about $3 billion of bonds. It estimated a $180 million profit, 110% on the $165 million it estimated BlackRock paid. All of Zambia's private lenders except Intesa Sanpaolo refused its September 2020 request to suspend payments. In Sri Lanka, Hamilton Reserve Bank of St Kitts and Nevis, holding more than $250 million of bonds, sued in New York in June 2022; its lawyers said the bonds are broadly held by US retirement systems including Fidelity, BlackRock and T. Rowe Price.

The law matters as well as the owner. In May 2020 Jubilee Debt Campaign counted 90% of the foreign currency bonds owed by the 77 countries in the G20's debt suspension scheme as governed by English law. That covers those bonds only, not all their debt, and the release does not say whether it counts bonds or dollars. In Mozambique, more than $2 billion was borrowed through special companies on purported state guarantees. In 2024 the English High Court found the debt was procured by bribery and corruption orchestrated by Privinvest and ordered it to pay nearly $2 billion; Mozambique had already settled with financial institutions (White & Case, Mozambique's lawyers).
patterns.implications:
On the 2025 estimates, a BlackRock spokesperson said the firm is a long-term investor acting as a fiduciary for clients, mainly people saving for retirement, and must act in their best financial interests (Brit Brief, citing The Independent). JP Morgan and Goldman Sachs did not respond, and UBS and PIMCO declined. On Zambia, Debt Justice says BlackRock did not answer its March 2022 request for comment, and prints an earlier BlackRock letter saying it remains "prepared to engage constructively" on a consensual restructuring. In September 2022 BlackRock said "our clients have already experienced losses" on Zambian debt, that "it would appear unlikely that the full value of the investments will ever be realised," and that it would approach a formal restructuring "constructively and in good faith" (Business Day). Kevin Daly of abrdn, chair of a bondholder committee estimated to hold about 45% of Zambia's international market debt, said a deep cut would be unacceptable to creditors and that Zambia needed an agreement "that is fair for all parties." Sri Lanka asked the New York court to dismiss Hamilton's suit, calling it an "apparent attempt to gain leverage over a nation in crisis and jump ahead of other foreign creditors."

In March 2023 a UK parliamentary committee said "legislation may be required to compel all creditors, including the private sector, to participate in debt relief." The UK government replied that it prefers a market-based approach, that "under 50 per cent of debt contracts are drawn up under UK law," and that legislating would likely move contracts elsewhere. Debt Justice answered that the market-based approach has failed and that its proposal would not stop new loans.

patterns.title: Secrecy and security in Chinese loan contracts
patterns.summary:
In 2021 AidData and its co-authors (Gelpern, Horn, Morris, Parks and Trebesch) published 100 contracts between Chinese state-owned lenders and governments in 24 developing countries, with a dataset of $36.6 billion in loans from 2000 to 2020. They report "unusual confidentiality clauses that bar borrowers from revealing the terms or even the existence of the debt," and security such as "lender-controlled revenue accounts." They also say cancellation, acceleration and stabilization clauses could let lenders influence borrowers' policies. Some contracts contain promises to keep the debt out of collective restructurings, called "no Paris Club" clauses. Co-author Scott Morris said: "That's a very striking prohibition, and it seems to run counter to the commitments the Chinese are making at the G20," and noted China might not enforce those clauses (Al Jazeera).

Kenya's railway loan is one dispute over these terms. Kenya borrowed Sh477 billion from China Exim Bank for its standard gauge railway. A parliamentary committee report said Kenya Railways and the Kenya Ports Authority had their assets used as collateral (Nation). A leaked audit reported by Business Daily said the government waived the port's immunity from seizure in 2013. Both governments deny the port was collateral. In a court ruling, Justice John Mativo said Kenyans have a right to know the collateral, and the Nation says the government did not obey the order to publish the contract. China's ambassador Wu Peng said Chinese law bars making such contracts public, and that no Kenyan assets were attached as collateral. Transport secretary Kipchumba Murkomen later released three documents with no details of the collateral; lawyer Ahmednasir Abdullahi said: "This isn't the SGR contract. This is one of the finance agreements." The loan agreement refers to long-term service purchase agreements on take-or-pay terms, and the Auditor-General found that disputes go to a Chinese arbitration body (Nation). In May 2026 Business Daily reported that the Court of Appeal had upheld a ruling ordering release, and that Kenya's top transport official argued release could cripple national transport policy.
patterns.implications:
Two writers, Huang Meibo and Niu Dongfang, replied in an article first carried by Global Times that the study's "argumentation method and process" lack scientific basis and "its conclusions are untenable." They write that "setting confidentiality clauses is a common practice for lenders," that "with few exceptions, creditors and sovereign debtors normally do not publish their contract texts in full," and that similar clauses appear in loans from France's AFD. They note that China is not in the OECD's reporting system and write that "it has no obligation to disclose its loan information." They call the study's reading of the no Paris Club clauses one-sided, and say Cameroon alone is too narrow a comparison. Reuters reported that China's foreign ministry did not immediately reply to its request for comment on the study.

The collateral claim is also disputed. The China Africa Research Initiative says the Auditor General wrongly labelled the ports authority a borrower and misunderstood how a waiver of immunity works (Maritime Executive). On Hambantota in Sri Lanka, whether Chinese debt forced the lease is disputed. Marina Rudyak writes that China did not lure Sri Lanka into a debt trap, that China Eximbank's port loans were typically at a fixed 2%, that Hambantota repayments were about 5% of Sri Lanka's yearly external debt, and, citing Sri Lankan economists, that the lease raised foreign money needed for about $5 billion of international bonds maturing in 2019-2022, not Chinese loans. Sri Lanka's finance minister had said the money would repay expensive foreign loans. The Sri Lankan prime minister said the partnership was needed to free the country from the port debt, as the map's case records. The announced stake and the signed one differ: Sri Lanka announced 80% in October 2016 (Rudyak), and the July 2017 agreement gave China Merchants 70% on a 99-year lease for $1.12 billion (Wikipedia).

patterns.title: Debt relief: the Paris Club, China and who goes first
patterns.summary:
The Paris Club is an informal group of creditor governments, dating to 1956, that reschedules loans together, case by case and tied to an IMF-backed programme. Lex Rieffel, a former US Treasury desk officer for it, writes that "China, however, is not a member," and lists it among ad hoc participants. He cites a study by Horn, Reinhart and Trebesch putting debt owed to China at $370 billion at end-2017, against $246 billion owed to the 22 Paris Club members. Among 73 countries in the G20's Covid suspension scheme, China held $108 billion of $524 billion in debt outstanding at end-2019 (20.7%), and about $12 billion of $46 billion in payments due in 2020.

He says China treats China Development Bank loans as commercial rather than official, prefers bilateral deals and does not disclose full details. The G20's Common Framework, agreed in November 2020, brought China and the Paris Club together under the rule that creditors give comparable treatment.

Zambia was the test. It missed a $42.5 million bond payment in November 2020. On 22 June 2023 France announced a deal to restructure $6.3 billion in loans from government creditors, $4.1 billion of it owed to China, over 20 years with three years' grace. The $6.3 billion is the amount of debt covered, not the amount forgiven; private creditors held another $6.8 billion (AP). Sri Lanka went a different way. On 26 June 2024 a committee of Paris Club creditors plus India and Hungary, co-chaired by India, Japan and France, agreed to restructure $5.8 billion in loans its members had made. The same day Sri Lanka reached a separate deal with China Exim Bank covering $4.2 billion of Chinese credit. Both are amounts of debt covered, not relief given. A $2.18 billion China Development Bank loan was not addressed (AFP via Kuwait Times). The committee said it looks forward to receiving "all information necessary for the OCC to ensure comparability of treatment." AFP reports this as a request for details of Sri Lanka's other deals, including with China.
patterns.implications: China's stated position is that multilateral lenders should share the losses. Foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said: "We call on multilateral financial institutions and commercial lenders, who are the main creditors for developing countries, to participate in developing countries' debt relief efforts," and that official bilateral loans related to China are "less than 5% of Ghana's external debt." Central bank chief Yi Gang said China "is willing to work with all parties to implement the Common Framework." The US and European governments have argued this would amount to a bailout for China (Reuters). China has also given some relief on its own terms: waiving 23 interest-free loans to 17 African states, and agreeing to co-chair Ghana's official creditor committee with France. Interest-free loans are under 5% of $843 billion in Chinese commitments from 2000 to 2017 (AidData via Reuters). US Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen said "the weight of default and a stalled debt restructuring process can bring suffering to ordinary families" (AP).

patterns.title: How much foreign investors take home, and to which countries
patterns.summary:
Foreign direct investment earns income for its owners, and part stays in the host country. UNCTAD, the UN trade and development body, reports $1.5 trillion of this income in 2011 on $21 trillion of investment, a 7% return: 8% in developing economies, 13% in transition economies and 5% in developed countries. Globally in 2011, nearly one-third stayed in host economies and two-thirds went back to investors.

Parnreiter and colleagues (ZFW, 2025), in a paper on Germany using IMF data for 2005-2022, put the global average share sent home at 63.2%, counting dividends. They find six countries took 87.6% of net profit inflows: the US alone 41.2%, then the Netherlands, Germany, Japan, France and the UK. On the losing side, 30 countries account for 84.0% of losses, and 44.1% of net outflows came from middle-income countries, including Russia (8.8%), Brazil (7.3%) and Nigeria (4.5%). Tax-friendly places such as Ireland (11.3%), Malta (3.2%), Hong Kong (3.1%) and Belgium (2.5%) make up 20.7% of net outflows; the authors say many of those profits actually began elsewhere.

For sub-Saharan Africa, the report Honest Accounts 2017, by Curtis and Jones of Jubilee Debt Campaign, uses 2015 figures where possible. It counts $32.4 billion in foreign companies' profits sent out, within $202.9 billion of total outflows against $161.6 billion of inflows.

How much is kept depends partly on the deal. In Zambia, privatisation set the mining royalty at 0.6% of gross earnings, one of the lowest rates in the world according to IPS, and corporate tax fell from 35% to 25%. IPS reports that the 1997 privatisation had a clause that "entrenched a 0.6 percent royalty for 15 years," a point made by Metorex's chief executive Charles Needham.
patterns.implications: UNCTAD also says retained earnings are highest in developing countries, at about 40% of FDI income in 2011, and that this is an important source of financing, while warning that not all of it becomes capital spending. It estimates foreign affiliates pay developing-country governments about $730 billion a year (reference year 2012), on average about 10% of government revenues. When Zambia proposed raising its royalty to about 3%, First Quantum and Metorex said they "will seek legal advice," and Needham said: "We would certainly have a very long discussion about whether (a review) would prejudice our rights." Honest Accounts itself says "it is not possible to be strict about what constitutes an 'inflow' and an 'outflow'."

patterns.title: Investment routed through tax havens, and the tax that goes missing
patterns.summary:
UNCTAD said in 2015 that about 30% of cross-border corporate investment passes through offshore hubs, and estimated developing countries lose about $100 billion a year in tax on investment linked to those hubs. Across developing economies, each 10 percentage points of offshore investment goes with a 1-point lower rate of return. IMF economists Damgaard, Elkjaer and Johannesen wrote in 2019 that phantom investment, money passing through empty companies, comes to $15 trillion, almost 40% of global FDI, up from about 30% less than a decade earlier. Luxembourg and the Netherlands host nearly half; with Hong Kong, the British Virgin Islands, Bermuda, Singapore, the Cayman Islands, Switzerland, Ireland and Mauritius, ten economies host over 85%.

Tax treaties are one route. Senegal ended its 2004 treaty with Mauritius in January 2020, saying it had cost $257 million in lost revenue over 17 years, and Zambia's cabinet ended its 2012 treaty in 2020, having given up taxes on interest and royalties paid across borders (ICIJ).

Inside a single company, the route can be a price. A pilot audit of Mopani Copper Mines in Zambia, majority-owned by Glencore, was done by Grant Thornton and Econ Poyry for the Zambia Revenue Authority, and a summary was published by NGOs in 2011. It said costs were about $381 million higher in 2007 than in 2005 and that "the Mopani cost structure cannot be trusted to represent the true nature of the costs." It put the copper revenue gap for 2003-2008 at about $700 million, said the price paid "seems to be determined by the parent company," and described hedges as "more equal to moving taxable revenue out the country than true hedging." Mopani paid no corporate tax, because of losses carried forward since 2000; the auditors questioned those losses.
patterns.implications:
Glencore said the audit was "based on broad and flawed statistical analysis and assumptions" and that "no transfer pricing has taken place." Mopani's chief executive Emmanuel Mutati called it "flawed and incomplete," saying it ignored that about half of Mopani's copper comes from third-party concentrates. Five NGOs complained to the Swiss and Canadian OECD contact points in April 2011. The OECD's page tags the case as concluded and does not state the outcome. Public Eye, carrying the account of the Berne Declaration, one of the five, says Glencore supplied Mopani's unpublished financial reports for 2006-2010 in summer 2012 and never answered questions sent in December 2012.

Mauritius's government called the ICIJ material "illegally obtained and tampered with" and the allegations "factually incorrect," and said sovereign nations freely sign tax treaties, which prevent double taxation. It says it meets the standards on transparency, and 41 of its 45 treaties are covered by the OECD's anti-avoidance instrument. Its revenue authority did not respond on Senegal or immediately on Zambia (ICIJ). UNCTAD says measures against offshore hubs "must include an investment policy perspective," and that work on avoidance needs added measures to sustain investment. The IMF authors note that empty companies pay their hosts for tax advice, accounting and registration.
